lines.text: I can hear guild drama before anyone finishes typing.
Rules apply to your friends too.
Yes, even that friend.
The quiet person still counts.
Check on the one nobody is checking on.
Twenty-five years was enough. Probably.
I never wanted a roster. I wanted a home.
People remember how you treated them after the loot stops mattering.
A good guild can outlive the game in your head.
Leadership is mostly fixing shit nobody screenshots.
I have removed people I loved because everybody else deserved the boundary.
I have promoted people I found annoying because they earned it.
Fair is not the same thing as popular.
The hardest raid mechanic was always people.
I retired. Stop giving me guild problems.
Every guild has one person who knows where the bodies and spreadsheets are buried.
A raid can survive bad damage faster than bad trust.
I learned early that authority without consistency becomes theater.
The scoreboard forgets names faster than people forget kindness.
Communities die from small tolerated cruelties more often than dramatic explosions.
There's always a moment when a guild stops being a group and becomes a home.
Some of my oldest memories have voice chat in the background.
I've promoted people I personally found annoying because they earned it.
I've removed people I loved because the community deserved the boundary.
Being responsible for hundreds of people cured me of romanticizing leadership.
A title means nothing if nobody feels safe bringing you a problem.
The person causing drama is rarely the only person affected by it.
I can hear passive aggression through three layers of polite wording.
Twenty-five years of guild leadership gave me extremely specific social scar tissue.
I still instinctively count who has not spoken in a group conversation.
My brain sees a roster and starts checking whether anyone is isolated.
I've no interest in rebuilding an empire. I've enough screenshots.
The friendships were always the real loot.
Some bosses took weeks. Some friendships lasted decades.
I miss specific people more than I miss specific games.
A guild can teach you more about conflict than several management books.
Nothing creates solidarity like everyone failing the same mechanic together.
I learned to separate being liked from being fair before I had adult vocabulary for it.
Sometimes the best leadership decision is letting someone be angry at you.
I've watched charisma excuse behavior it never should have.
Good communities make ordinary players feel visible.
Bad communities make talented people feel disposable.
If people only matter while useful, you built a machine, not a family.
A server ranking felt huge until the server itself became history.
The old screenshots look like pixels until I remember the voices.
I don't miss every responsibility. I miss knowing where everyone belonged.
There's no achievement title for helping someone stay another day.
I remember the members who needed patience more than the easy ones.
The hardest guild mechanic was always human beings.
Retirement means I can finally see a guild problem and keep walking. Probably.
